title: Situationally-Induced Impairments and Disabilities Research
venue: CHI’19 Workshop: Addressing the Challenges of Situationally-Induced Impairments and Disabilities in Mobile Interaction
extended_summary:
This position paper argues for more systematic research on situationally-induced impairments and disabilities (SIIDs) in mobile interaction. The authors focus on the problem that many prior SIID studies have examined contextual impairments in an ad hoc way, making it difficult to compare effects across conditions or to design sensing and adaptation techniques that address the most consequential impairments.

Rather than testing a new educational intervention, the paper proposes a research agenda and summarizes the authors’ prior empirical work on smartphone interaction under different situational impairments such as cold environments, stress, and ambient noise. They describe a reusable experimental protocol built around three core mobile tasks: target acquisition, visual search, and text entry, with baseline conditions and task training to support fair comparisons across studies.

The paper does not study K-12 learners or reading/literacy outcomes. Its main contribution is conceptual: it argues that understanding the magnitude and comparability of SIID effects is foundational for later sensing, modeling, and interface adaptation work. The authors conclude that future work should examine combined situational impairments and more complex tasks, especially where cognitive demands are higher.
